claims.text: The density and distribution of inclusions and irregular grain boundaries in bare Q235 steel govern early passive-film formation and stability.
A more uniform Q235 microstructure promotes rapid and continuous passivation.
Rapid, continuous passivation suppresses localized pitting in chloride-containing environments.
Microstructural heterogeneity causes localized passive-film breakdown and accelerates corrosion degradation.
Polishing and thermal pretreatment or annealing can reduce surface microstructural heterogeneity by homogenizing inclusion distribution and grain-boundary character.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution is an applicable corrosion-test environment for Q235-based specimens.
The proposed mechanism applies at room temperature and approximately 70°C.
The passive layer formed on Q235 steel is likely composed of Fe3O4 and/or Fe2O3.
Passive oxide forms more uniformly on homogeneous surface regions and is disrupted at localized anodic sites associated with heterogeneity.
Regions containing clustered non-metallic inclusions or irregular grain boundaries act as localized anodic sites.
Localized anodic sites hinder formation of a coherent passive film.
A more uniform surface accelerates and stabilizes passivation, thereby altering local electrochemical behavior and overall corrosion kinetics.
Surface-treated Q235 samples will form a more continuous and protective oxide film than untreated samples.
Surface-treated Q235 samples will exhibit lower corrosion current density and higher charge-transfer resistance than untreated samples.
Surface-treated Q235 samples will exhibit less mass loss and reduced pitting than untreated samples.
The predicted treatment benefit will occur at both room temperature and moderately elevated temperature.
The proposed behavior is expected in aggressive chloride environments below 100°C, where oxide formation and breakdown are especially sensitive to local microstructure.
The quantitative corrosion response may depend on residual stress, inclusion chemistry, and atmospheric oxygen.

Failure of treated specimens to show statistically significant improvement in corrosion current, charge-transfer resistance, mass loss, and pitting relative to untreated controls would falsify the hypothesis.
